profile.name: Charleston Stroll
profile.tagline: The high-kicking, syncopated rhythm dance born of Black dockworkers and 1920s jazz.
profile.insight: Danced at speeds up to 300 beats per minute, the Charleston set a 2018 world record when 1,096 dancers gathered in Shrewsbury to kick in unison.
profile.profile: The Charleston emerged from African-American dance roots and dockworker rhythms into a global sensation following the 1923 Broadway show Runnin' Wild. Named after the South Carolina harbor city, it features fast forward and backward kicks, twisted ankles, and expressive arm swings. The dance evolved from 1920s solo and partner formats into 1930s swing integration with Lindy Hop. Today it remains a vital fixture in swing dance communities worldwide.
profile.profile_long:
The Charleston originated in African-American tradition, tracing elements back to plantation dances such as the Juba as well as challenge steps like the Jay-Bird. Pianist and composer James P. Johnson noted hearing its core rhythm from Black dockworkers in Charleston, South Carolina, and observed early versions danced as early as 1913 at the Jungles Casino in New York City's San Juan Hill neighborhood. After appearing in Irving C. Miller's show Liza in early 1923, the dance gained nationwide fame when Johnson's tune 'The Charleston' featured in the Broadway musical production Runnin' Wild later that year. Between 1926 and 1927, the dance reached its international peak, spreading quickly across American speakeasies and European cabaret stages such as Paris, where Josephine Baker popularized it.

At its core, the movement mirrors a natural walking action executed in place or traveling along a floor. Dancers bend their knees slightly, turning feet inward and outward to alternate between knock-kneed and bow-legged positions while maintaining angled ankles. Kicks launch forward and backward, paired with swinging arms bent at ninety-degree angles at the elbows and wrists. In partner formations, couples dance in closed position, side-by-side, or tandem arrangements, counting an eight-beat movement cycle built around weight transfers and toe touches. Fast solo 1920s Charleston is characterized by high tempos often exceeding 200 to 300 beats per minute, punctuated by slower dragging steps or theatrical improvisations.

The dance's signature music incorporates hot jazz, stride piano, and ragtime rhythms driven by a syncopated clave beat closely related to the habanera. Women dancing the Charleston in the 1920s wore short dresses trimmed with ribbons, fringe, sequins, or perky tassels designed to accentuate body movement, alongside garçonne haircuts. Men typically wore dark pinstripe suits paired with neckties or bowties. Danced socially in speakeasies, formal contests, and modern jam circles, the Charleston historically represented a spirit of post-World War I independence and playful defiance against moral regulation.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance traces back to traditional African-American plantation dances like the Juba and challenge step routines. James P. Johnson recalled hearing its signature beat from dockworkers in Charleston, South Carolina, and seeing early iterations around 1913 at the Jungles Casino in New York's San Juan Hill. Willie 'The Lion' Smith recalled a predecessor performed by Russell Brown under the name 'Geechie dance'. It debuted on stage in Irving C. Miller's Liza in spring 1923 before exploding in popularity through the Broadway production Runnin' Wild, which ran from October 28, 1923 to June 28, 1924. Peak popularity hit between mid-1926 and 1927, making it a global symbol of the Roaring Twenties.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Charleston can be danced solo, with a partner, or in group lines and circles. Dancers maintain slightly bent knees with feet turned inward and outward, creating alternating knock-kneed and bow-legged positions while keeping feet at right angles to the leg at the ankle. The arm action mirrors natural walking: as the left leg steps forward, the right arm moves forward while bent at the elbow and wrist. The standard 8-count basic footwork involves touching one foot behind without shifting weight on counts 1–2, placing weight onto that foot on 3–4, touching the opposite foot forward on 5–6, and returning to standing position on 7–8.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for the 1920s Charleston features early hot jazz, ragtime, and stride piano played at rapid tempos ranging from 50 to 75 bars per minute (200 to over 300 beats per minute). The fundamental rhythm incorporates the syncopated clave beat, which composer Gunther Schuller linked to the habanera and the Spanish Tinge. Primary instrumentation includes stride piano, brass, reeds, and swing rhythm sections.
sections.costume_and_setting: During the 1920s, women wore short flapper dresses or skirts adorned with hanging ribbons, fringe, sequins, or feathers designed to highlight dynamic leg and hip movements, paired with short 'à la garçonne' hair. Men wore black pinstriped suits with bow ties or neckties. Settings ranged from Broadway theaters and Parisian cabarets to American speakeasies, floor contests, and public stunts.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a casual social and challenge dance among African-American communities, the Charleston became an emblem of post-WWI liberation, youth culture, and defiance of alcohol prohibition in American speakeasies. In contemporary swing dance culture, it functions as both a high-energy solo showpiece and a core element within Lindy Hop social dancing and jam circles.
sections.notable_figures: Key historic figures include composer James P. Johnson, performer Elisabeth Welch, dancer Russell Brown, cabaret star Josephine Baker, film stars Bessie Love, Ann Pennington, Ginger Rogers, Joan Crawford, and dancers Santos Casani and Josie Lennard.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include 1920s Solo Charleston, 20s Partner Charleston, 30s/40s Partner Charleston (incorporating jockey, side-by-side, and tandem positions), Collegiate Charleston, Crawl Charleston (a 1933 slow variation resembling a tango or waltz), and Black Bottom.
sections.lineage: Rooted in African-American Juba and dockworker rhythms, the Charleston evolved through 1920s stage revues into social partner and solo forms. In the 1930s and 1940s, it integrated into Lindy Hop and swing jazz, serving as a direct ancestor to Quickstep and modern Jazz Roots.

basic_steps: Stand with knees slightly bent and feet turned slightly inward at ankles.
On counts 1-2, step or touch the left foot back without shifting full weight.
On counts 3-4, step onto the left foot, shifting full body weight onto it.
On counts 5-6, touch the right foot forward while swinging left arm forward with bent elbow.
On counts 7-8, bring the right foot back into standing position, shifting weight to repeat.
teaching.rhythm: 4/4 meter with syncopated clave rhythm, typically 50 to 75 bars per minute.
teaching.formation: Solo, paired in closed/jockey/side-by-side/tandem position, or group lines and circles.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on the 8-count weight shifts and arm-leg counter-swing before accelerating to high tempos and adding twisting footwork.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Syncopated 4/4 rhythm incorporating the clave beat and stride piano syncopations.
music_profile.vocal_style: Vivid solo or chorus revue singing; often purely instrumental stride or hot jazz.
music_profile.musical_form: 32-bar AABA or ABAC jazz structures with repeating rhythmic phrases.
music_profile.sound_description: Bright stride piano bass chords on downbeats matched with syncopated treble accents, driving brass melodies, and rapid banjo or drum backbeats.

movement_profile.posture: Upright torso with slight forward pitch; knees constantly flexed; ankles relaxed to allow inward/outward foot rotation.
movement_profile.footwork: Alternating weight transfers, toe touches forward and back, inward (knock-kneed) and outward (bow-legged) ankle twists.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Arms swing in counter-motion to legs, bent at 90 degrees at elbows and wrists; palms facing down or out.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Torso pulses rhythmic isolation; hips twist naturally with leg movement and foot rotation.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Danced in place, traveling in stroll lines, or arranged in social circles and jam formats.
movement_profile.partnering: Closed position, jockey position, side-by-side hold, or tandem (one dancer in front of the other holding hands at hip height).

signature_moves.name: Basic 8-Count Step
signature_moves.description: Touch foot back on 1-2, step on 3-4, touch foot forward on 5-6, step back on 7-8 while swinging arms.

signature_moves.name: Savoy Kicks
signature_moves.description: High forward and backward swinging kicks executed during 8-count footwork.

signature_moves.name: Johnny's Drop
signature_moves.description: A sudden knee drop or lowered accent performed during a freeze phrase.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Low to medium knee flex; occasional hop transitions or showy stunt jumps in jam circles.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid stiff knees or rigid ankles; avoid locking joints during rapid leg twists and high kicks.

episode_brief.title_hook: Twisting Feet and Fast Kicks: The Birth of the Charleston
episode_brief.logline: Trace how African-American plantation steps and Harlem stride piano sparked a global dance craze that defined the 1920s.
beats: Open on archival footage of 1920s dancers and dockworkers in Charleston, South Carolina.
Demonstrate James P. Johnson's signature stride rhythm on piano.
Break down the basic 8-count footwork step by step in slow motion.
Show partner holds: closed, side-by-side, and tandem positions.
Explore the 2018 Guinness World Record gathering in Shrewsbury with over 1,000 dancers.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the basic 8-count walking and weight-shifting pattern in place.
drills: Practice touch-step forward and back slowly without music.
Add 90-degree elbow arm swings in opposition to leg movement.

lesson_ladder.goal: Incorporate foot twisting (inward/outward rotation) and increase tempo to 200 BPM.
drills: Alternate knock-kneed and bow-legged ankle twists on each count.
Execute basic steps while traveling forward and backward.

lesson_ladder.goal: Perform high kicks, tandem partner turns, and solo jam circle improvisations.
drills: Drill Savoy kicks on counts 5 and 6 at 250+ BPM.
Transition fluidly between solo 20s Charleston and side-by-side partner holds.

visual_motifs: Close-up shots of twisting feet and ankle angles.
Fringe and ribbon momentum on 1920s dresses.
Pianist hands flying across stride piano keys.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An energetic swing historian and master dancer who combines precise technical footwork breakdowns with lively historical storytelling.
episode_brief.music_cue: Fast 1920s stride piano track starting at 220 BPM with heavy syncopated clave accents.

connections.name: Lindy Hop
connections.note: Charleston steps were integrated directly into Lindy Hop during the 1930s and 1940s.

connections.name: Black Bottom
connections.note: A contemporary 1920s trend featuring similar binary syncopated rhythms and hopping steps.

connections.name: Quickstep
connections.note: Collegiate Charleston served as a direct precursor to the ballroom Quickstep.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the 8-count pattern seated in a sturdy chair, tapping toes back on counts 1-2, weight placing on 3-4, tapping forward on 5-6, and returning on 7-8 while swinging bent arms.
seniors.standing_version: Perform the basic 8-count step while holding onto a balance barre or chair back, omitting ankle twisting and keeping kicks low.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduce music tempo to 100-120 BPM and keep foot taps within a tight 12-inch range.
seniors.counts: 1-2 touch back, 3-4 step down, 5-6 touch front, 7-8 step down.

children.game_version: Charleston Freeze Tag: Children dance the basic step in a circle and must freeze in a bow-legged or knock-kneed position when the music stops.
children.counts: 1-2 touch back, 3-4 step down, 5-6 kick front, 7-8 step back.
avoid: Overly high tempos above 200 BPM during initial learning

gaps: Specific footwork variations for the Charleston Stroll formation relative to general 1920s Charleston basic steps are limited in the provided broad text.
